The parents report that she has always been small for her age, but they have become increasingly worried as she seems to have fallen further behind her peers in height and weight over the past year.

Her appetite is poor, and she appears fatigued.

Blood in stool
The patient is an 8-year-old female with a known history of Celiac Disease, Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, and Sturge-Weber Syndrome who returns to the Gastroenterology clinic for further evaluation.

She was last seen in this department six months prior for concerns regarding poor growth and persistent abdominal pain, and continues to receive multidisciplinary care for her complex medical conditions.
The parents report that approximately three weeks ago, they began to notice streaks of bright red blood on the surface of her stool.
Initially they attributed this to constipation, though the child has continued to have normal, well-formed bowel movements without straining.
Over the past two weeks, her mother has observed that the patient has become increasingly fatigued with decreased energy during play.
Her teachers have also commented that she often appears pale compared to her classmates.
The patient has complained intermittently of abdominal pain, sometimes localizing to the periumbilical region.
Her appetite has decreased slightly, and she frequently refuses to finish meals.
Upon further questioning, the parents note that several dark spots on her lips have been present since she was a toddler; these spots have persisted over the years and have become slightly darker.
They initially believed these were freckles, but have also observed similar spots on the inside of her cheeks.

The father recalls undergoing multiple colonoscopies in his 20s and 30s for removal of intestinal polyps.
A paternal aunt was diagnosed with breast cancer in her late 30s.
The paternal grandfather died of pancreatic cancer in his 50s.

No other siblings are affected.
The family is concerned that the daughter may have inherited a condition that “runs in the family.”
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: Never. Occupation: Student.
There has been no nausea or vomiting.
There has been no recent fever, cough, or upper respiratory illness.
Her vital signs are within normal limits.
On physical examination, the child appears slightly underweight for her age.
Her weight is at the 20th percentile, whereas it was previously closer to the 50th percentile a year ago.
Her conjunctivae appear pale.
Oral examination reveals multiple 2- to 3-mm pigmented macules on the buccal mucosa and on the vermillion border of the lips.
There are no ulcers or vesicles.
Her abdomen is soft, with mild tenderness in the periumbilical region.
There is no rebound or guarding.
There are no palpable masses.
There is no hepatosplenomegaly.
Rectal examination reveals normal sphincter tone and no masses.
The stool sample is guaiac-positive.
Laboratory testing shows hemoglobin of 9.0 g/dL, hematocrit of 27%, and mean corpuscular volume of 71 μm³.
Leukocyte and platelet counts are normal.
Iron studies are consistent with iron deficiency anemia.
An abdominal ultrasound is unremarkable.
The patient undergoes colonoscopy for further evaluation.
The procedure reveals multiple pedunculated polyps scattered throughout the colon.
Several similar polyps are visualized in the distal small intestine.
The largest polyp measures 1.3 cm.
Three polyps are removed for histopathology.
The parents are referred to genetic counseling for confirmation and family screening.
The child is started on iron supplementation for anemia.
A follow-up plan is arranged with pediatric gastroenterology and oncology.

encounters.cc: Recurrent episodes of fever and joint pain

lines: Recurrent episodes of fever and joint pain

This 8-year-old female with a history of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, celiac disease, and Sturge-Weber syndrome, previously evaluated for nutritional rickets, chronic abdominal pain, and gastrointestinal bleeding, presents with recurrent episodes of fever and joint pain.
Her parents report that over the past month she has had daily high fevers, usually peaking in the late afternoon or evening, that resolve spontaneously by the next morning.
These fevers are often accompanied by a pink, blotchy rash on her trunk and upper limbs that appears and disappears with the fever spikes.
The rash is non-pruritic and does not leave marks.
She also complains of joint pain in her knees and wrists that worsens in the morning and improves throughout the day.
She has become more fatigued and has missed several days of school.

encounters.cc: Ongoing joint symptoms and persistent fatigue

lines: Ongoing joint symptoms and persistent fatigue

The patient is a 10-year-old female with established systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, celiac disease, and nutritional rickets who presents to the hematology clinic for ongoing evaluation of joint symptoms and persistent fatigue.
She has been followed longitudinally in rheumatology for recurrent fevers and arthralgias, with her most recent rheumatology evaluation approximately six months prior for similar concerns.
Her parents report that she has had multiple episodes over the past 4 months of joint pain and stiffness, especially in the knees, wrists, and ankles.
The joint pain is worse in the mornings and often causes difficulty getting out of bed or walking to school.
They have also noticed that her energy levels are lower than those of her peers and that she takes frequent naps after school.
She occasionally develops a pink, patchy rash on her chest and abdomen that seems to worsen with fever and fades spontaneously.
The rash is non-pruritic and does not leave marks.
She has no known allergies, recent infections, or sick contacts.
Her appetite has declined, and her weight is below the 10th percentile for her age.
